Q: Memory Leak in Next.js Application – How to Diagnose and Fix? A:

The comments already point pretty clearly to the server, so I’d avoid starting with the browser and first make sure the process itself is actually retaining memory.

A couple of things matter here because heapUsed alone can be misleading.

First, measure the process after it has warmed up. Don’t compare startup memory with memory after a few requests.

Second, run Node with --expose-gc and call global.gc() before taking the samples. Otherwise you can easily mistake normal GC behaviour for a leak.

I’d also keep an eye on rss and arrayBuffers, not just heapUsed. A process can keep growing outside the V8 heap, so a flat heapUsed doesn’t necessarily mean everything is fine.

For the actual test, I’d isolate the routes. Start a fresh process, hit one route repeatedly, force GC between samples, and look at the post-GC trend. Then do the same with the next route. That makes it much easier to tell which route is actually responsible instead of looking at the whole application as one big number.

Once you have a route that consistently grows after GC, take two heap snapshots: one early in the run and another after the memory has grown. You can generate them with v8.writeHeapSnapshot() or attach the inspector with NODE_OPTIONS=--inspect and use the Memory tab in Chrome DevTools.

The useful part of the snapshot isn’t just finding a large object. It’s finding out why it is still reachable. For example, if you see objects retained through a Timeout, that points you towards things like setInterval/setTimeout that aren't being cleaned up. In the Typesense case, I’d follow the retainer chain from the growing objects back to the client, cache, listener, or whatever is keeping them alive.

The important distinction is basically:

  • heapUsed grows and keeps growing after GC → likely JS/V8 retention.
  • rss grows while heapUsed stays relatively stable → look outside the V8 heap.
  • arrayBuffers grows → investigate buffers/native-backed memory.
  • Everything stabilises after GC → probably normal allocation/GC behaviour rather than a leak.

And I’d test each route in a fresh process. Otherwise a leak from a previous route can contaminate the measurements and make the results much harder to interpret.

For reference, I built next-leak to automate pretty much this loop for Next.js apps (App Router, output: "standalone", Node 22+). It runs each route in a fresh process, forces GC before sampling and gives you a per-route result:

npx next-leak .

https://github.com/xabierlameiro/next-leak

Q: Using fractions and greek letters in ggplot annotations, what works and what doesn't A:

If you're familiar with LaTeX, the latex2exp package might help.

library(ggplot2)
#> Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.2.2
library(latex2exp)

# define expression
exp_text <- r'($30 \degree$,  $\frac{11 \pi}{6}$)'

# make plot
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = 0, 
      y = 0, 
      xend = 0.866, 
      yend = 0.5
    )
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "text",
    x = 0.3,
    y = 0.25, 
    label = TeX(exp_text)
  )
#> Warning in is.na(x): is.na() applied to non-(list or vector) of type
#> 'expression'

Q: How to understand this Java code that produces DOM output? A:

A javax.xml.transform.Transformer transforms (as it's name implies) a javax.xml.transform.Source into a javax.xml.transform.Result, possibly applying an XSL Stylesheet in the process. The source code lines around the transformer are

Transformer transformer = TransformerFactory.newInstance().newTransformer(); // line 3
transformer.transform(domSource, sr); // line 6

Now, what is the source in your code example? Its 

...Document newDoc... // line 1
DOMSource domSource = new DOMSource(newDoc); // line 2

meaning: a javax.xml.transform.Source implementation that reads a org.w3c.dom.Document.

The javax.xml.transform.Result is:

StringWriter sw = new StringWriter(); // line 4
StreamResult sr = new StreamResult(sw); // line 5

meaning it is a javax.xml.transform.stream.StreamResult (consisting of a stream of characters or bytes) that writes into a java.io.StringWriter.

In the end, the result that has been written into the java.io.StringWriter is output on the console:

System.out.println(sw.toString()); // line 7

Q: How to read and write XML files and treat the comment nodes as text nodes in Java when saving A:

Don't use indent="yes" if you want the output to be identical to the original. Specifying indent="yes" allows the serializer to insert whitespace pretty-well anywhere it wants.

Q: How does the processor handle conditions? A:

The processor has "Branch if" instructions that when a certain condition is met it branches, and otherwise it continues on to the next instruction.

So

if(A)
{
    dosomething;
}

would become

load A into register 0
if the zero flag is set (ie, register 0 contains 0x00) then jump to endcondition)
dosomething
endcondition:

More complex conditions ( if(A || B && C) ) become a sequence of instructions that leaves a register in a 0 or non zero state, so the branchif instruction can jump or not jump based on the conditional flags.

There are many conditional flags (zero, carry, negative, overflow, etc), and some branchif instructions also operate on more complex conditions (ie, it might actually check to see if a register is equal to another register, rather than simply looking at flags). Each architecture is different and makes tradeoffs so the instruction set is complete, but also speedy and compact.

As moocha points out in the comments, some architectures allow you to apply a conditional to some, many, or even all instructions, so you might not only have 'branch if' instructions, but also 'and if', 'add if', 'move if' etc.

The x86 is very, very, very complex beyond this simple explanation once you get into pipelining, out of order execution, caching, microcode, and all the other advanced topics. For most purposes the above explanation is sufficient. If you're writing a hand crafted very, very tightly wound algorithm, though, you'll have to take these things into account for maximum performance and throughput.

That's a topic for another question though...

Q: How to create an image displayer using Python Tkinter more efficiently? A:

This is because when photo is not global it is garbage collected by the python garbage collector hence you need to keep reference to the image, this can be done so by saying global image or label.image = photo. Either way you just have to keep a reference so that it is not garbage collected.

global might not be efficient with OOP as it could create some issues later, is what i heard, so you can keep a reference by label.image = photo.

From effbot.org:

The problem is that the Tkinter/Tk interface doesn’t handle references to Image objects properly; the Tk widget will hold a reference to the internal object, but Tkinter does not. When Python’s garbage collector discards the Tkinter object, Tkinter tells Tk to release the image. But since the image is in use by a widget, Tk doesn’t destroy it. Not completely. It just blanks the image, making it completely transparent.
